findings.title: Permission-denial cache can reintroduce the exact staleness bug the PR is meant to fix
findings.body: In Check(), after the early permDenialCache short-circuit (lines 116-121), a negative Check() result (resource not found in the cached permission map) causes a fresh DB query and, if still denied, a new entry is written to permDenialCache with shortCacheTTL (30s) (lines 153-155). If any Check() call is evaluated for a given (user, action, name, parentFolder) tuple shortly before the underlying resource becomes visible/granted (e.g. a speculative/early access check, or a check issued immediately after creation but before permissions/propagation settle), that negative result is now cached explicitly for up to 30s and will short-circuit all subsequent checks for that exact resource during that window — even though the resource now exists and the user should be allowed. This can resurrect, in a narrower but still real window, the exact 'user can't access the item they just created' problem this PR is meant to solve, because the explicit denial cache is not invalidated when the underlying permission/permCache is refreshed.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric mislabels cache hits that end up denied as cache misses
findings.body: When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission map (err == nil) but checkPermission on it returns false, the code does not record a cache hit; it falls through to line 137 which unconditionally increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false" (cache miss), even though the cache was actually consulted and hit. This understates the true cache hit rate for any action whose cached permission set does not include the requested resource, which will skew cache-hit-rate dashboards/alerts used to tune cache TTLs or diagnose cache effectiveness.

findings.title: Negative results no longer short-circuited by the main permission cache, risking repeated DB round-trips per distinct resource
findings.body: Previously, a cached permission map that didn't grant access to a specific resource was enough to return 'denied' without hitting the DB. Now, any cache hit that evaluates to 'not allowed' triggers an unconditional DB refetch of full identity permissions (getIdentityPermissions) before the result can be cached per-resource in permDenialCache. For a legitimately-denied identity, every distinct (name, parentFolder) combination requested during the permDenialCache TTL window (30s) incurs one full DB permission query (basic role + teams + permissions) the first time it's seen, since the per-resource denial cache has not yet been populated for that specific resource/folder pair. A client enumerating many resource names (or polling many different items the user has no access to) can therefore generate significant extra DB load compared to before this change.

findings.title: Unescaped delimiter concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey risks ambiguous cache keys
findings.body: userPermDenialCacheKey builds the cache key by joining namespace, userUID, action, name, and parent with plain "_" separators without escaping or using a fixed-width/length-prefixed encoding. Because four variable-length segments (action, name, parent) are concatenated with the same separator, different combinations of these values that happen to contain "_" (or produce the same concatenated string through different splits) can collide into the same cache key, returning a cached allow/deny decision for the wrong resource. While action strings and most Kubernetes names are unlikely to contain underscores today, this is a fragile key-construction pattern that silently depends on that external invariant holding.
